rv.q: 'The King and I' arrives like the ship that heaves into the Beaumont stage: a majestic vessel, bringing many wonderful things. Sher directs with palpable respect and a care to avoid orientalist humbug...You marvel at the sophistication of the theme: intercultural change and evolution. This 'King and I' speaks a universal language of love.
This production is a welcome testament to the power of delicacy in the age of the hard sell.
I doubt I'll see a better production of 'The King and I' in my lifetime.
Chalk up another triumph for Theater.
Now the same creative team, including star Kelli O'Hara, has reassembled to do it again, magnificently, with "The King and I."

Now comes And I, in one of the most elegantly beautiful and beautifully sung productions I’ve ever seen, and the Beaumont looks like a living treasure chest for a director with the right vision and a company that can command a vast space and make it feel like your living room.
In any case, the revival that opened tonight, in a Theater production directed by Bartlett Sher and starring Kelli O’Hara and Ken Watanabe, is too beautiful to miss.
It will stay contentedly aloft for the next 2 hours and 50 minutes.
This Broadway revival of Rodgers and Hammerstein's 1951 musical is a sumptuous production that respects the original while finding ways to make it feel fresh.
This revival is a gorgeous, sumptuous production that honors the original while making it feel fresh and relevant for today's audiences.

If you loiter on the Lincoln Center Plaza late most evenings, you can watch the audience dispersing from the latest revival of that mid-20th century modern masterpiece The King and I. And you can bet that plenty of them are whistling a happy tune. Of course, there’s little to fear in any new staging of the 1951.
This lavish revival of Rodgers and Hammerstein's 1951 musical is a feast for the eyes and ears, with Kelli O'Hara delivering a luminous performance as Anna.
O'Hara is perfectly suited to her role as a prideful Englishwoman, and sings rapturously throughout the show, especially on her poignant renditions of "Hello, Young Lovers."
Those looking for a time-honored Broadway musical realized on a grand scale could do no better.
There are moments in Theater's ravishing new Broadway production of The King and I (***½ out of four) that may leave you grinning so hard your face will hurt.

This 'King and I' is excellent...The production has the epic sweep that the authors intended...Sher and his leading players also investigate undercurrents of romance and physical attraction which were not evident in the original production...Sparks fly.
Everyone in this immense company performs to perfection, starting with Kelli O’Hara - a giant star radiating warmth with that crystalline voice.
O’Hara could bring out the romantic swoon in just about any male costar, and Anna is another triumph in her winsome recent gallery of fine portrayals.
"The King and I" requires a regal, charismatic leading lady, and in O’Hara, it has one who's just about perfect.
From the very first moments of Lincoln Center’s ravishing The King and I, it feels like a privilege just to be sitting in the audience.
Sher once again reveals the musical's own enormous qualities without imposing an arbitrary interpretation
And just like that, this splendid revival emerges as majestic and intimate simultaneously.
This remains a production in which all aspects have been satisfyingly thought out, and a work that stands the test of time.

"Their sparring match is at the true heart of any production of this show, and it’s a little bit of a rocky fight for a while…But somewhere in the second act, as their characters’ hearts begin to melt for each other – and so do ours - these performers simply sail into the theatrical stratosphere…If you’re not sniffling a little at the final curt...
“The King and I” holds up incredibly well as a piece of drama.
This musical is so glorious that I was moved to tears on a few occasions.
The King and I, a beloved classic given an extravagant production.
It merely fulfills virtually every reasonable expectation of Rodgers and Hammerstein fans who hope to be delighted anew with a familiar classic on Broadway.
Director Bartlett Sher has done a brilliant job – you almost see him waving a conductor's wand over the pageantry.

cn.t: Lincoln Center's sumptuous revival earns widespread acclaim for its visual splendor and Kelli O'Hara's radiant performance, though a few critics find the production overly respectful and note chemistry issues between the leads.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
